# Compare Spring Boot layered and executable JAR container images

This runbook packages a simple Spring Boot Web Application into two container
images and compares the effect of copying the application as one executable JAR
versus copying it as Spring Boot layers.

A standard Spring Boot executable JAR contains the application classes, Spring
Boot loader, and dependency JARs in one archive. That is convenient to run, but
it is a poor fit for Docker layer caching: when a small application class
changes, the Dockerfile copies a new JAR, so the image layer containing the
entire archive changes too.

A layered JAR keeps the same executable application but exposes groups of files
that change at different rates. By default, Spring Boot separates dependencies,
Spring Boot loader classes, snapshot dependencies, and application code. A
Dockerfile can then copy stable dependency layers before the frequently changing
application layer. The result is not a different application; it is a container
image layout that lets Docker reuse more unchanged layers across rebuilds.

This example focuses on how Spring Boot layers affect Docker’s ability to reuse
unchanged image layers. It does not cover every aspect of running Java in
containers, including runtime privileges, image signing, vulnerability scanning,
observability, and deployment hardening. For a more holistic example that
combines several concerns, see
[all-in-one-spring-boot](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md).

You will inspect the JAR’s layer layout and compare image histories and file
groups from two Dockerfiles built from the same application JAR and JDK image.
The application exposes one endpoint that returns a random quote from its
embedded database.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- inspect the layers in a Spring Boot executable JAR;
- build layered and single-JAR images from the same application artefact;
- compare how the Dockerfiles place application files in image layers; and
- explain when finer Docker cache reuse justifies a more involved Dockerfile.

## Prerequisites

Use this example directory for the commands below. Java 25, a running Docker
daemon, `curl`, `jq`, and `tree` are required. The included Maven wrapper
supplies the Maven version used for the application build. Dive is optional and
is used only for visual inspection of the built images. Port 8080 must be
available for the optional local and container runtime checks.

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) runtime

- `curl`, used to call the Spring Boot endpoint.

- `jq`, used to format the JSON response returned by the application.

- `tree`, used to inspect generated directories in the walkthrough.

- [Dive](https://github.com/wagoodman/dive), or a similar tool, is optional
  and used only when visually inspecting image layers.

### Oracle Container Registry access

Before pulling an Oracle Java base image, sign in to Oracle Container Registry
and accept the terms for the
[Oracle Java JDK repository](https://container-registry.oracle.com/ords/ocr/ba/java/jdk).

1. Accept the Oracle Container Registry terms.

2. Authenticate your container engine with your own Oracle Container Registry
   username and authentication token.

   Pass the token through standard input so it is neither recorded in shell
   history nor copied into the project or image layers. If you use Podman, use
   its equivalent `login --password-stdin` command.

   ```shell
   docker login container-registry.oracle.com \
     --username 'ALBERT.ATTARD@ORACLE.COM' \
     --password-stdin < ~/.ocr/auth-token
   ```

   This should print the login succeeded message.

   ```shell

   ```

   Docker pulls the image if necessary, then prints the Java runtime version.

   ```

   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   ```

## The artefacts to inspect

The Spring Boot application packages its quote endpoint, database migration,
launcher, and dependencies into one executable JAR. The Maven build produces
`target/layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar`; both Dockerfiles consume that same
file and use the same Oracle JDK 25 base image. The layered Dockerfile extracts
the JAR’s logical groups and copies them separately into the final image. The
single-JAR Dockerfile copies the executable archive in one step. Inspect the two
Dockerfiles before building so the later image histories have a clear source.

- The layered container

  ```dockerfile
  FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 AS builder
  WORKDIR "/opt/app"

  ARG JAR_FILE="./target/layered-jar-spring-boot-*.jar"
  COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]
  RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar "app.jar" extract --layers --destination "extracted"

  FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
  WORKDIR "/opt/app"

  COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/extracted/dependencies/", "./"]
  COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/extracted/spring-boot-loader/", "./"]
  COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/", "./"]
  COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/extracted/application/", "./"]

  EXPOSE 8080

  ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
  ```

- The fat-JAR container used for comparison

  ```dockerfile
  FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
  WORKDIR "/opt/app"

  ARG JAR_FILE="./target/layered-jar-spring-boot-*.jar"
  COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

  EXPOSE 8080

  ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
  ```

## Build the application

The application is built once and then reused for the local runtime checks and
both container images. This matters because the comparison should isolate the
runtime packaging choice, not a different application build.

1. Build the application

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   The build should create `target/layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar`.

   (*Optional*) List the build output to verify the input used by all later
   steps.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. (*Optional*) Run the application

   This confirms that the packaged JAR works before the container steps add
   Dockerfiles and image layers to the picture.

   The application is started in the background for convenience, otherwise the
   subsequent commands need to be executed in another terminal.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   Wait until the endpoint responds successfully; this establishes that the
   packaged JAR serves requests before container packaging is introduced.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote. A JSON response confirms that the local JAR can serve
   the same endpoint later checked in the images.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Winston Churchill",
     "id": 185,
     "quote": "Attitude is a little thing that makes a big difference."
   }
   ```

   Stop the local process to free port 8080 for the later runtime checks.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

## Guided walkthrough

Run the following steps from `examples/layered-jar-spring-boot`. The Maven build
above provides the same JAR for the extraction and both image builds. The local
extraction shows the file groups; the image histories then show how each
Dockerfile places those groups into image layers.

### Inspect the layered JAR

The commands below use the JAR produced in
[Build the application](#build-the-application). Inspect its logical layers,
then extract and reassemble their contents to see what the layered Dockerfile
copies into its final image.

1. (*Optional*) List the layers available

   The `tools` jar mode used here supersedes the older `layertools` mode in
   [Spring Boot 3.3](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/wiki/Spring-Boot-3.3.0-M3-Release-Notes#deprecations-in-spring-boot-330-m3).

   ```shell
   java \
     -Djarmode=tools \
     -jar './target/layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' \
     list-layers
   ```

   This application uses the four default layers.

   ```
   dependencies
   spring-boot-loader
   snapshot-dependencies
   application
   ```

   The layer groups are configurable. See
   [Custom Layers Configuration](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/maven-plugin/packaging.html#packaging.layers.configuration)
   of the Spring Boot documentation for more information about this.

2. Extract the artefacts from the executable JAR file

   The executable JAR contains dependency JARs, the Spring Boot launcher,
   application classes, and configuration and migration resources.

   The `extract --layers` command writes each logical layer to a separate
   directory under `./target/extracted`. Keeping the extracted files under
   `./target` makes the runbook repeatable and keeps generated build artefacts
   away from source files.

   Look for the four layer directories after extraction. Their contents are the
   inputs to the layered Dockerfile’s separate copy steps.

   ```shell
   java \
     -Djarmode=tools \
     -jar './target/layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' \
     extract --layers --destination './target/extracted'
   ```

   (*Optional*) Inspect the extracted directories and their files.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name './target/extracted'
   ```

   Spring Boot writes a separate directory for each logical layer. In current
   Spring Boot versions, each layer may contain JAR files rather than only
   expanded class directories.

3. Copy the artefacts

   The extracted artefacts are grouped into layers. This directory structure is
   useful for Docker copy instructions, but it is not the final runtime layout.
   The contents of each layer directory are copied into one application
   directory (`./target/app/`) in the same order used by the Dockerfile.

   Compare the copied order with the
   [Spring Boot Dockerfile example](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/packaging/container-images/dockerfiles.html).

   ```shell
   DESTINATION='./target/app/'
   rm -rf   "${DESTINATION}"
   mkdir -p "${DESTINATION}"
   cp -R './target/extracted/dependencies/.'          "${DESTINATION}"
   cp -R './target/extracted/spring-boot-loader/.'    "${DESTINATION}"
   cp -R './target/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/.' "${DESTINATION}"
   cp -R './target/extracted/application/.'           "${DESTINATION}"
   ```

### Compare the container images

Both Dockerfiles use the JAR produced in
[Build the application](#build-the-application) and the same JDK base image.
Their application copy steps are the variable to compare. Image history and
optional Dive inspection show the resulting layer structure; a single build does
not measure cache savings on subsequent builds.

1. Build the Layered JAR container image

   This Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build. The builder stage extracts the
   Spring Boot layers from the executable JAR. The final stage copies those
   extracted layers one by one, creating Docker layers that line up with the
   Spring Boot layer model.

   ```dockerfile
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 AS builder
   WORKDIR "/opt/app"

   ARG JAR_FILE="./target/layered-jar-spring-boot-*.jar"
   COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]
   RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar "app.jar" extract --layers --destination "extracted"

   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
   WORKDIR "/opt/app"

   COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/extracted/dependencies/", "./"]
   COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/extracted/spring-boot-loader/", "./"]
   COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/", "./"]
   COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/extracted/application/", "./"]

   EXPOSE 8080

   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
   ```

   The order in which the layers are copied is very important as the layers that
   change the least are copied before those that change more frequently. Docker
   can then reuse the dependency and loader layers when only application code
   changes, and rebuild only the later application layer.

   Build the container image and load it into the local docker daemon.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-Layered-Jar' \
     --tag 'demo:layered-jar' \
     --load \
     .
   ```

   The first build may need to pull the base image and execute all copy steps.
   Later rebuilds can reuse unchanged lower layers. The build output and history
   show which steps exist; they do not quantify a time saving here.

2. Analyse the Layered JAR container image

   List the layers that were added by the Dockerfile.

   ```shell
   docker history 'demo:layered-jar'
   ```

   The history should show separate copy steps for the Spring Boot layers.

   ```
   ID            CREATED                 CREATED BY                                     SIZE        COMMENT
   08ff276e6fd9  Less than a second ago  /bin/sh -c #(nop) ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-ja...  0B
   ```

3. (*Optional*) Run the Layered JAR application

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --detach \
     --name 'layered-jar' \
     --publish 8080:8080 \
     'demo:layered-jar'
   ```

   Wait for HTTP 200 from the containerised application before fetching a quote.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote to verify that the layered image serves the endpoint.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Henry Ford",
     "id": 75,
     "quote": "The only real mistake is the one from which we learn nothing."
   }
   ```

   Stop the container to free the port for the single-JAR image.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'layered-jar'
   ```

4. Build the Fat JAR container image

   This Dockerfile copies the executable JAR as one file and runs it with
   `java -jar`. It is simpler, but any application change produces a different
   JAR file, so Docker has to replace the whole application copy layer.

   ```dockerfile
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
   WORKDIR "/opt/app"

   ARG JAR_FILE="./target/layered-jar-spring-boot-*.jar"
   COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

   EXPOSE 8080

   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
   ```

   This Dockerfile uses the same JDK image and JAR input as the layered version.
   Its single application copy step provides a useful contrast in image history.

   Build the container image and load it into the local docker daemon.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-Fat-Jar' \
     --tag 'demo:fat-jar' \
     --load \
     .
   ```

   Build time depends on local cache and network state. Compared with the
   layered version, later rebuilds have less cache granularity because the
   complete executable JAR is copied again whenever its contents change.

   layer to cache or replace.

- [Spring Boot Maven plugin: packaging and layers](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/maven-plugin/packaging.html#packaging.layers)
- [Docker: understanding image layers](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/building-images/understanding-image-layers/)
- [Docker: build cache](https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/)

## Key takeaways and trade-offs

- The JAR exposes four logical Spring Boot layers; the layered Dockerfile copies
  their files in separate image steps.
- Both images run the same application from the same JAR and JDK base image.
  Their image histories differ in how application content is grouped.
- Separate copy steps can let Docker reuse unchanged dependency layers after
  application-only changes, at the cost of a more involved Dockerfile.
- Inspect actual rebuilds and deployment needs before choosing a layout; this
  walkthrough does not measure speed gains or establish production readiness.
